new.why: NVIDIA’s October 21 release supplies a new open stack and explicit evaluations connecting retrieval choices with agent task success and token use.
new.summary: Multimodal agent retrieval combines visual-text embedding, relevance reranking and structured document parsing so agents can locate evidence across charts, tables and scans.
new.why_now: NVIDIA published dated models, methods and benchmark results on October 21, establishing a concrete first Watchlist baseline for this pipeline.
new.practical_value: Teams can benchmark each stage separately on their own documents, measuring relevance, downstream task success, token use and serving throughput.

evidence.title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Embed, Rerank, and Parse

novelty.reason: The release unifies multimodal embedding, reranking and structured parsing as separately deployable components for agent evidence pipelines.

evidence.reason: NVIDIA publishes model variants, evaluation methods, benchmark tables and throughput figures, although all headline results remain publisher-run.

independence.reason: Public benchmarks enable outside testing, but the reviewed release and its measured claims originate from NVIDIA and collaborators.

momentum.reason: No stable comparable deployment metric has two source-linked observations at distinct times, so momentum remains unestablished.

relevance.reason: Teams can directly benchmark relevance, task success, token cost and throughput on their own visually rich document collections.

durability.reason: Separating retrieval, reranking and parsing remains useful even as particular models, indexes and accelerator generations change.

momentum.reason: No stable comparable deployment metric has two source-linked observations at distinct times, so momentum remains unestablished.

updated.what_changed: Salesforce adds a new no-code CRM implementation with explicit draft, review, test, permission and publication stages.
updated.summary: Reusable agent Skills package repeatable instructions, context and tools that assistants can discover and apply to bounded work without restating every step.
updated.why_now: Salesforce’s Winter ’27 release adds dated evidence for drafting through Coworker and governing reuse through Skill Builder.
updated.practical_value: Sales operations teams can test one account-review Skill on safe records, inspect permissions and approve the procedure before wider distribution.

evidence.title: Build and Use Reusable Agentforce Skills

novelty.reason: Salesforce extends reusable Skills into a no-code CRM workflow with drafting, review, testing and controlled publication stages.

evidence.reason: Official release and Help material document the procedure and permissions, but provide no independent comparative effectiveness evaluation.

independence.reason: Salesforce adds a distinct enterprise implementation to prior AWS, Google, NVIDIA and Plaud publisher evidence for reusable Skills.

momentum.reason: The implementations report unlike capabilities rather than one comparable numerical measure observed at distinct valid timestamps.

relevance.reason: Sales operations teams can immediately test one bounded account-review routine on safe records before approving organization-wide reuse.

durability.reason: Reviewable instructions, limited tools, controlled testing and publication remain durable requirements across assistant products and interfaces.

momentum.reason: The implementations report unlike capabilities rather than one comparable numerical measure observed at distinct valid timestamps.

updated.what_changed: Anthropic moves permission boundaries into a proactive assistant preview that names actions requiring confirmation before execution.
updated.summary: Consumer task agents need minimum authority, visible connected sources, enforceable action limits, reconstructable histories and human escalation for consequential work.
updated.why_now: Claude Duet’s October 21 preview adds a second publisher implementation with approvals before messaging, payment, signing and deletion.
updated.practical_value: Individuals can write allowed, confirmation-required and prohibited actions before connecting an assistant, then audit briefs and execution histories.

novelty.reason: Claude Duet applies familiar permission ideas to proactive daily briefs and consequential consumer actions in a managed environment.

evidence.reason: Anthropic specifies approval categories, access limits and known miscalibration risk, but the preview lacks independent outcome evaluation.

independence.reason: Anthropic provides a second publisher implementation alongside the earlier AWS control framework, though both remain publisher-authored evidence.

momentum.reason: The sources describe different controls without two comparable numerical observations, so a directional momentum score is unsupported.

relevance.reason: Ordinary users can convert the named approval boundaries into a concrete checklist before connecting a proactive assistant.

durability.reason: Least authority, confirmation for consequential actions and reviewable histories remain durable regardless of assistant branding or model.

momentum.reason: The sources describe different controls without two comparable numerical observations, so a directional momentum score is unsupported.

carried_forward.why: The October 20 release remains the latest concrete primary evidence, and no dated independent comparison was found during this refresh.
carried_forward.summary: Priority-aware inference operations coordinate queueing, cache placement and service isolation so shared model fleets can honor differentiated workload objectives.
carried_forward.why_now: This topic is carried while teams need independent reproduction of llm-d v1.0 fairness, cache and zero-downtime operating claims.
carried_forward.practical_value: Inference operators can replay mixed-priority traffic and measure latency, starvation, cache effectiveness and rollout disruption before production enablement.

evidence.title: llm-d v1.0: State-of-the-Art Inference Ready for Day 2

novelty.reason: The release combines explicit workload priority, fairness and cache-aware routing within one operational inference framework.

evidence.reason: The October 20 release documents mechanisms and one cache result, while detailed independent reproduction remains unavailable.

independence.reason: The evidence comes from project maintainers and participating vendors, without an independent comparative production study.

momentum.reason: One release observation provides no repeated comparable service metric at distinct valid observation times.

relevance.reason: Inference operators can directly test latency, starvation, cache effectiveness and rollout continuity under mixed-priority traffic.

durability.reason: Queue fairness, cache placement and safe rollouts remain durable concerns across models, accelerators and serving stacks.

carried_forward.why: Meta’s October 19 report remains the current primary case, and today’s research found no independent reproduction requiring reclassification.
carried_forward.summary: Thin orchestration boundaries keep central agents focused on routing and typed handoffs while specialists retain narrow context and tools.
carried_forward.why_now: This topic is carried pending evidence from another organization that measures route accuracy, revision rates and specialist-boundary failures.
carried_forward.practical_value: Agent teams can compare one broad agent with deterministic routing, typed handoffs and explicit revision measurements on representative work.

novelty.reason: The architecture sharply limits the orchestrator to deterministic routing and typed coordination instead of generalized execution.

evidence.reason: Meta supplies architecture details, workflow counts and internal delivery observations, but not a reproducible external benchmark.

independence.reason: All measured results originate from Meta’s internal environment and lack independent replication across another organization.

momentum.reason: Reported outcomes do not form two comparable observations under one stable measure at distinct timestamps.

relevance.reason: Teams facing context collisions can directly test route clarity, handoff completeness, revisions and specialist tool boundaries.

durability.reason: Separation of coordination and execution should persist, although optimal specialist granularity will vary by workflow.

dropped.summary: Open-weight coding models require explicit checkpoint, precision, sharding, cache, runtime and hardware choices before meaningful evaluation.
dropped.why_now: The topic is dropped after the refresh found no independent quality, latency, throughput or cost replication beyond its original publisher.
dropped.practical_value: Readers can retain the deployment checklist for future evaluations without treating one vendor guide as evidence of broad operational momentum.

previous_evidence.title: Introducing Reflection Beam, an open-weight model for agentic coding on AWS

novelty.reason: A large open-weight model focused on agentic coding adds a configurable alternative to managed proprietary endpoints.

evidence.reason: AWS documents architecture, checkpoints and multiple deployment paths, but supplies no independent task-quality benchmark in this guide.

independence.reason: Current implementation evidence is entirely AWS and Reflection authored, with no separately operated deployment evaluation reviewed.

momentum.reason: One release guide cannot establish directional change in adoption, performance, operating cost or deployment reliability.

relevance.reason: Engineering teams can reproduce configuration tests and measure quality, latency, throughput and resource requirements before adoption.

durability.reason: Checkpoint portability and transparent serving choices remain useful even as particular runtimes and accelerator generations change.
